poiBRA-desc:
Brazil is a harsh military dictatorship, with its government and populace blaming all their misfortunes on the Andean Compact, their most direct neighbor, with the use of state propaganda.

The Andean Compact has on several occasions been accused of exploiting the continent, especially lithium, by moving the wealth out of it, impoverishing the rest of the countries and condemning them to hell.

Brazil believes that only through a strong reaction can the tyranny of the Andean Compact be halted.

Seeing as most of the little wealth and resources that Brazil has left has been invested in its military in anticipation of a potential war with the Compact, Brazil certainly has the capability of throwing the entire region of South America into needless conflict.

But the regime's grip is weaker than its arsenal suggests. In 2198, General Manuel Branco Velho overthrew President {{poiBRA012|Frederico Watanabe}} in a coup, and the elected government has spent the years since in exile in Lima, kept alive by Andean aid and claiming to be the true Brazil. In what remains of the Amazon, the Lamentadores wage a decades-long guerrilla war against the state in the name of the rainforest. In the backwoods, the Legião Sertão, a warlord's army remade in flesh and steel, answers to no flag but its commander's. Brazil's enemies are not only across the border.
poiBRA001-desc:
Hear, hear, citizens of Brazil! The future of your great nation lies in your hands. This year will decide our fate. Shall we come together as a nation? Put aside our petty differences? Unite against hate and injustice? Shall we fight in unity against the corrupt forces of the Andean Compact?

Will you, citizen, allow your entire family to be massacred by the Andeans? Would you watch them nerve staple your children and trample on your country's flag? Go! Pick up a weapon, a spade, a hammer! Go to the front, to the factories, do not fear. When we are one, we are indestructible.
poiBRA002-desc: In the aftermath of the 2198 coup, Manuel Branco Velho and his clique of supporters have plotted and tried everything in and beyond their power to save the regime. However, rampant deterioration of the Amazon rainforests, the collapse of order in urban centers, and the failure of the Space Campaign have taken their toll. The Brazilian people yearn for peace and accept slow rebuilding. But the regime still has an ace up its sleeve...
poiBRA003-desc: The Brazilian army suffers from rampant unprofessionalism, with most of its rank-and-file consisting of conscripts and former criminals pressed into service. While officer corps remain some of the best on the continent, they can only do so much when the soldiers under their command are completely lacking in discipline. If Brazil is to survive the coming war with the Compact, then these grunts must be hammered into shape.
poiBRA004: Army of Lions, Led by Lions
poiBRA004-desc: General Rejinaldo de Alencar has always been a force for innovation within Brazil's infamously conservative military. As commander-in-chief, de Alencar intends to transform the Brazilian Armed Forces into an elite force without equal.
poiBRA005-desc: Despite their origins as a bunch of backwoods militias, the Legião Sertão has wholeheartedly embraced {{poiBRA011|Eloa Alvarez}}'s philosophy of transhuman darwinism. Many Legionaries have enthusiastically taken to modifying themselves with combat genes, black-market bionics, and military grade cybernetics, all in the pursuit of transforming themselves into apex predators.
poiBRA006-desc: The industrialists of Brazil have always been supportive of Frederico Watanabe's free market policies, especially compared to the stifling dirigisme of the military regime. Many prominent businessmen followed Watanabe into exile after the Coup of '98, and have remained close allies of the president upon his return to Brazil.
poiBRA007-desc:
Although it is the democratically elected government of Brazil, many remain unconvinced that President Watanabe is anything more than an Andean puppet. The fact that the Brazilian administration has spent two years in exile in Lima has only strengthened this notion, not to mention the fact that they are still reliant on Andean aid.

To regain the support of the people, they will need to demonstrate that its forces fight for liberty and democracy rather than foreign interests. They have to prove that the legitimate government can stand on its own two feet and fight for its people.
poiBRA008-desc:
The Lamentadores have spent decades fighting a guerrilla war against the Brazilian state in what remains of the Amazon jungle. Although the clique was founded with lofty ideals in mind, years of non-stop insurgency have pushed it further and further from its idealistic origins. They walk a fine line between crusading a noble cause and giving to brutal pragmatism.

Its founder, {{poiBRA010|Lucio Ximenes}}, still holds to those ideals, but he is old, and the commanders who will inherit his militia grew up in the war rather than the cause.

Right now, the people view the Lamentadores as little more than terrorists. Its forces are merciless, and it still relies on underworld contacts to keep the lights on. While its enemies fear them, so do the Brazilian people. The Lamentadores are a long way from cementing their image as a legitimate force for good in Brazil
poiBRA009-desc:
General Manuel Branco Velho had always stood apart from the rest of Brazil's military elite. Where most commissioned officers were the sons of generals and oligarchs, Velho enjoyed no such privilege as the fourth son of a Cuiabá handyman. Like many in the favelas, Velho and his brothers left for the army at a young age in pursuit of a better life.

During the Cerrado War, Velho lost all but one of his brothers in the war against the guerrillas, yet gained a reputation as a model soldier who never flinched in the face of the enemy. His heroic actions during Operation Navalha caught the attention of his commanding officers, who then acted as his patrons during his rise to the Brazilian High Command during the 2170s.

An avowed Brazilian nationalist, General Velho was the driving force behind the Coup of '98 that overthrew President Frederico Watanabe for his connections with the Andean Compact. Declaring a state of emergency soon after, he then focused on restoring the prominence of the Brazilian Armed Forces in preparation for the eventual war with the Compact, claiming them to be both the main threat to Brazilian sovereignty and the main obstacle to Brazilian prosperity.

While his critics paint Velho as yet another opportunistic dictator, he maintains that he has always been a man who has stopped at nothing in service of his fatherland. Everything that General Velho has done has been in the name of reasserting Brazil's status as a global power by any means necessary.
poiBRA010-desc:
It was once said that the first person who will live 150 years has already been born. There are more than a few who think that Ximenes will hold that title. Born in Brazil during the Dark Age, Ximenes grew up seeing the consequences of humanity's destruction of the environment first hand. Once he came of age, he took a job in academia, travelling across South America, learning of the continent's rich culture and history. He had hoped that through this scholarship, the solution for mankind's failure could be found. He was wrong. Years of travel and research made him realise that Brazil needed more than philosophers to save the Amazon. That was when he met Eloa Alvarez.

Alvarez grew fond of such an educated man, and brought Ximenes into their survivalists group of insurgents who sought to preserve the Amazon through action not words. For a time, Ximenes went along with this group and happily helped in their mission. But as the years went on, he began to see Alvarez not as a liberator, but a semi-fascist autocrat. With a heart heavy from the many crimes he had committed, Ximenes deserted the group, taking many like minded followers with him.

Ximenes spent the next few decades forming his own survivalist militia, the Lamentadores, revealing himself as a gentle man with a kind heart. Many flocked to his side, viewing him as the best chance for Brazil to save itself, both culturally and ecologically. His reluctance to use the underhanded tactics of other factions only added to his appeal.

But now, at over a century old, with his dream of a green Brazil finally within reach, it is feared he will not live to see it. The man who once led entire platoons of soldiers and guerrillas can now only walk with the assistance of a cane. Even the advanced medicine and technology of this era can give him only a few more years. With the Grim Reaper fast approaching, Ximenes plans to use his skills as much as he can, so that when he finally does depart this world, it will be a better place than when he entered it.
poiBRA011-desc:
Eloa Alvarez is yet another leader among the many figures of South America, but even among the harsh survivalists of the region, she is notorious for her rigid beliefs, staunch belief in might-makes-right, and a fearsome military.

The military in question is composed mostly of fellow survivalists—they are drawn to power like moths, and Eloa bears the torch of strength. Even for them her practices are brutal, and this brutality enforces her will over theirs. Survivalists are loyal, but that loyalty is only to power. A sign of weakness, and the warriors may leave to stronger rulers still—or deem themselves stronger instead. Survivalists are both a source of strength, and what tests it. Often, signs of mercy may be a weakness in the eyes of those who find mercy an alien thing, and there will be time for mercy once the work is done.

Her history is usually kept private—she sees no reason to share it—but it is generally understood she grew up among the lower classes along the northern outskirts of Brazil, the tumultuous border regions of her country. Raiders, bandits, and survivalists often raided her home, making each day a question of life and death. Her father was the only notable figure in her life, an old soldier who fought in a forgotten war. Despite his efforts, his beliefs contrasted with what Eloa saw—and she saw violence.

Violence breeds violence, and the womb of war bred something far worse than petty thieves and lost warriors robbing families—it bore Alvarez, and at her command was all the horrors her army could muster.

It began as a cause. Alvarez once led insurgents who meant to save the Amazon from those who were burning it, and among her lieutenants was a scholar named Lucio Ximenes. But every victory taught her the same lesson: the jungle belonged to those strong enough to keep it. Mercy cost her fights, so she dropped it. The scholar left, and she did not mourn him. Slowly the forest stopped being the goal and became the pretext, and the cause became the army itself. In time she found the creed that justified what she had become, that the strong should remake themselves into something stronger still, in flesh and in steel. That creed is what the Legião Sertão now preaches.

She was borne by the sword, and was forced to live by it, and now she must ensure no other weapon may pose a threat to her people, her people of many blades.
poiBRA012-desc:
Frederico Campos Watanabe was the last President of the Seventh Republic. In 2196 he announced the Campanha Espacial, the Space Campaign: with investors from the Andean Compact, Brazil would turn {{poiBRA013|the Amazon Sea}} region into South America's first major spaceport, an undertaking he promised would both revive and modernize the economy.

Instead it became a political disaster. The megastructures were stalled again and again by natural disasters, logistical failures, strikes and investors pulling out, leaving Brazil to foot much of the bill while the country around it kept getting worse. Many accused Watanabe of putting the interests of the Andean elite above those of his own people, and the loudest voices came from the fiercely nationalist Armed Forces. In 2198, as rumours of a budget cut rippled through the ranks, General Manuel Branco Velho and his clique of officers marched on Brasilia, deposed Watanabe and restored military rule.

Watanabe and his supporters fled to Lima, where they lead the Governo Republicano Provisório in exile. To them he is the rightful president of a free Brazil, and they wait for the day the junta overreaches, when the old republic can return with Andean support and volunteers from around the world. To Brasilia, he is the Compact's puppet, and the best proof that the Andes want Brazil on its knees.
poiBRA013-desc:
Shortly after the Great Mistake, the Amazon Sea began to form. At first there were reports of minor flooding in the heart of the jungle. Then the rivers overflowed. By the time anyone understood what was happening, the government was too busy with the worldwide economic collapse to deal with it.

Today the Amazon Sea is a grim reminder of what happens when a country forgets its environment. The land is not all the state forgot. Indigenous groups, anti-government guerrillas and refugees from Bolivaria have lived there in poverty and anarchy since the Great Mistake, and a century of neglect has bred a deep hatred in them. Dissidents, political enemies, deserters and misfits have flowed into the northwest for generations.

The region is now effectively outside government jurisdiction. Tax collection stopped in the 2160s, and the last resident governor was evacuated by helicopter in 2189. Survivalist cliques thrive in the rainforest and have begun linking up with their counterparts on the northern coast.
poiBRA014-desc:
Before the Great Mistake, the Sertão was a modest desert in Brazil's northeast, sparsely inhabited and always on the back burner of politics. Few presidents ever bothered to secure it against rebellion. As the climate deteriorated, the Sertão began swallowing the lands around it, and today most of the northeast is desert, a natural refuge for dissidents ready to take up arms against the regime.

Patrolling it is nearly impossible. The government holds the region behind the Salles Line, but the desert's people know it far better than the army does and can move through it at astonishing speed. If civil war comes, the general staff does not expect to hold the north for more than a few weeks.
